title: Implement `iv_*_includes()` family
description:
Closes https://github.com/DavisVaughan/ivs/issues/41

---

As much as I didn't want to create a new function family, nothing else made enough sense.

`iv_between(needles, haystack, flip = TRUE)` is ok, but it is hard to describe and I don't like that the returned vector length matches `haystack`. Also `iv_locate_between(needles, haystack, flip = TRUE)` would return a data frame with `"needles"` and `"haystack"` columns that would be flipped from how they align with the inputs, which I found confusing.

`iv_within()` and `iv_contains()` are nice ideas too, but it was tough to find a universal way to allow both vector and iv inputs as `needles` (or as `haystack` for `iv_contains()`). We also have to consider the rare case where you could theoretically have some nested structure like `iv_within(<iv>, iv<iv<>>)` where the lhs `<iv>` is actually treated like a vector. This is super rare, but the fact that you can do this with `iv_includes()` makes me think it is slightly more correct.


---

Solving the SO issue mentioned here https://github.com/DavisVaughan/ivs/issues/41#issue-1506221033

``` r
library(ivs)

df1<-data.frame(diveno=c(1,2,3,4,5), 
                start=c("2018-08-01 08:20:40","2018-08-01 08:40:50", "2018-08-01 10:01:00","2018-08-01 15:45:30","2018-08-01 17:06:00"),
                fin=c("2018-08-01 08:39:20","2018-08-01 08:53:40","2018-08-01 10:16:30","2018-08-01 15:58:20", "2018-08-01 17:18:20"))

df1$start <- as.POSIXct(df1$start,format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",tz="CET")
df1$fin <- as.POSIXct(df1$fin,format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",tz="CET")


df2<-data.frame(date=c("2018-08-01 08:30:00", "2018-08-01 15:47:00", "2018-08-02 17:10:00"))
df2$date <- as.POSIXct(df2$date,format="%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S",tz="CET")

iv_includes(iv(df1$start, df1$fin), df2$date)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE
```

---

And the other SO question mentioned here https://github.com/DavisVaughan/ivs/issues/41#issuecomment-1434762963

``` r
library(dplyr)
library(ivs)
library(lubridate)

table <- tibble( 
  start = as.Date(c("2022-08-02", "2022-10-06", "2023-01-11")), 
  end = as.Date(c("2022-08-04", "2023-02-06", "2023-02-04"))
)

events <- c(
  ymd("2022-08-07"), 
  ymd("2022-10-17"), 
  ymd("2023-01-17"), 
  ymd("2023-02-02")
)

table %>%
  mutate(range = iv(start, end), .keep = "unused") %>%
  mutate(count = iv_count_includes(range, events))
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>                      range count
#>                 <iv<date>> <int>
#> 1 [2022-08-02, 2022-08-04)     0
#> 2 [2022-10-06, 2023-02-06)     3
#> 3 [2023-01-11, 2023-02-04)     2
```

description:

title: Add `vec_ptype()` and `vec_ptype_finalise()` methods
description:
Closes #27 
Closes #33

See the benchmark in #27 for the performance rationale.

This also fixes a bug I found in #33 that had to do with the fact that `vec_ptype()`'s default fallthrough calls `vec_slice()`, which will finalise. This meant that previously `vec_ptype(iv(NA, NA))` was returning `iv<logical>` rather than `iv<unspecified>`, which practically meant that these couldn't be combined `vec_c(iv(NA, NA), iv("x", "y"))`.

I've also had to switch from `vec_ptype2()` to `vec_ptype_common()` in a few places, because I want a finalised ptype and the former doesn't finalise. In a similar way, I've had to follow up some calls to `vec_ptype()` with `vec_ptype_finalise()` to ensure I return a finalised ptype.

CC @lionel-. We've been talking about whether or not `vec_ptype()` should return a finalised ptype. I'm actually not sure if it should, because writers of S3 methods like my `vec_ptype.ivs_iv` method need to somehow be able to write a method that returns an unspecified inner type when needed (so it can be reduced correctly in `vec_ptype2()`), and if `vec_ptype()` always finalised then I wouldn't be able to do that correctly. I think we just have to be extra careful about following up bare calls to `vec_ptype()` with `vec_ptype_finalise()` in rare cases where it is needed.

title: Implement family of container functions
description:
Closes #20 
Depends on https://github.com/r-lib/vctrs/pull/1644

Solving the original issue posted in #20 is now straightforward with `iv_identify_container()`, which works nicely here because each interval maps to exactly 1 container.

``` r
library(ivs)
library(dplyr, warn.conflicts = FALSE)

dat <- tibble(
  time_left = as.Date(c(
    "2011-08-05","2011-07-25","2011-07-25","2017-08-20",
    "2017-08-20","2017-10-09","2011-07-25",NA,NA,"2019-06-01","2019-06-01"
  )),
  time_right = as.Date(c(
    "2011-09-14","2017-09-02","2017-09-01","2017-09-12",
    "2017-09-26","2017-10-15","2017-09-02",NA,NA,"2019-11-05","2019-11-05"
  )),
  x = c(114, 120, 20, 10, 1, 5, 200, 5, 10, 100, 130)
)

dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(
    time = iv(time_left, time_right),
    .keep = "unused",
    .before = 1
  )

dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(container = iv_identify_container(time), .after = time)

dat
#> # A tibble: 11 × 3
#>                        time                container     x
#>                  <iv<date>>               <iv<date>> <dbl>
#>  1 [2011-08-05, 2011-09-14) [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02)   114
#>  2 [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02) [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02)   120
#>  3 [2011-07-25, 2017-09-01) [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02)    20
#>  4 [2017-08-20, 2017-09-12) [2017-08-20, 2017-09-26)    10
#>  5 [2017-08-20, 2017-09-26) [2017-08-20, 2017-09-26)     1
#>  6 [2017-10-09, 2017-10-15) [2017-10-09, 2017-10-15)     5
#>  7 [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02) [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02)   200
#>  8                 [NA, NA)                 [NA, NA)     5
#>  9                 [NA, NA)                 [NA, NA)    10
#> 10 [2019-06-01, 2019-11-05) [2019-06-01, 2019-11-05)   100
#> 11 [2019-06-01, 2019-11-05) [2019-06-01, 2019-11-05)   130

dat %>%
  group_by(container) %>%
  summarise(x = max(x))
#> # A tibble: 5 × 2
#>                  container     x
#>                 <iv<date>> <dbl>
#> 1 [2011-07-25, 2017-09-02)   200
#> 2 [2017-08-20, 2017-09-26)    10
#> 3 [2017-10-09, 2017-10-15)     5
#> 4 [2019-06-01, 2019-11-05)   130
#> 5                 [NA, NA)    10
```

When a single interval falls in multiple containers, an error is thrown from `iv_identify_container()`. You have to use `iv_identify_containers()` if you really want to handle this kind of thing.

``` r
library(ivs)

x <- iv_pairs(c(1, 6), c(2, 8), c(2, 3))
x
#> <iv<double>[3]>
#> [1] [1, 6) [2, 8) [2, 3)

iv_identify_container(x)
#> Error in `iv_identify_container()`:
#> ! Intervals in `x` can't fall within multiple containers.
#> ℹ Location 3 falls within multiple containers.
#> ℹ Use `iv_identify_containers()` to identify all of the containers that a particular interval is contained by.

iv_identify_containers(x)
#> <list_of<iv<double>>[3]>
#> [[1]]
#> <iv<double>[1]>
#> [1] [1, 6)
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> <iv<double>[1]>
#> [1] [2, 8)
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> <iv<double>[2]>
#> [1] [1, 6) [2, 8)
```

title: Use splits and groups naming conventions
description:
```r
iv_splits()
iv_identify_splits()
iv_locate_splits()

iv_groups()
iv_identify_group()
iv_locate_groups()
```

Removed what would be `iv_locate_group_bounds()`, as that doesn't seem useful.

Also, `iv_locate_groups()` now returns the result of `iv_groups()` in the `key` slot, rather than the integer locations that you'd use to slice with. This is more consistent with `iv_locate_splits()`
